Repeat victimisation: how often the same targets are victimised again

Source: R/rptvic.R
rptvic.Rd

Asks how much crime falls on targets (people, households, addresses, businesses) already victimised, and how soon a repeat follows. From one record per incident with the target's identifier (and its date):

Usage

rptvic(id, t = NULL, pop = NULL, brk = NULL)

Arguments

id

The target of each incident: labels.

t

NULL or the time of each incident: numbers (days, say).

pop

NULL or the number of targets at risk: one number, at least the number of victims.

brk

NULL or the edges of the intervals of time since the previous incident: increasing numbers, two at least (needs t).

Value

An object of class rptvic, a list: tab, one row per number of victimisations k (from 0 with pop): victims, incidents and, with pop, expected, the Poisson's victims; stat, a named vector: incidents, victims, repeats, rshare, conc, incid and prev (NA without pop), rvict (victims with two or more), erep (the Poisson's number of them) and ratio; gap, NULL without t, otherwise n, mean and median of the times between successive incidents; and lag, NULL without brk, otherwise one row per interval (lo, hi, n, share, cum).

Details

  • incidence, prevalence and concentration (Trickett, Osborn, Seymour and Pease 1992): incidents per target at risk, victims per target at risk, and incidents per victim; and the repeats, the incidents beyond each victim's first, with their share of all incidents;

  • the victims by number of victimisations, against the numbers a Poisson count with the same mean over the pop targets at risk would give: more victims with two or more than the Poisson expects (ratio above 1) is victimisation concentrated beyond chance, the classic finding for burglary;

  • the time between a target's successive incidents: their number, mean and median, and with brk the share of repeats falling in each interval since the previous incident, which for burglary is highest soon after (Johnson 2008).

A count of victims misses the targets never victimised: pop supplies them. The Poisson comparison assumes every target has the same risk, so it measures how far risk varies, and does not by itself tell a target's lasting attractiveness ("flag") from a first incident raising the risk of the next ("boost").

References

Trickett, A., Osborn, D. R., Seymour, J. and Pease, K. (1992). What is different about high crime areas? The British Journal of Criminology, 32(1), 81-89. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.bjc.a048181

Johnson, S. D. (2008). Repeat burglary victimisation: a tale of two theories. Journal of Experimental Criminology, 4(3), 215-240. doi:10.1007/s11292-008-9055-3

Farrell, G. and Pease, K. (1993). Once Bitten, Twice Bitten: Repeat Victimisation and its Implications for Crime Prevention. Crime Prevention Unit Series Paper 46. Home Office, London.

Examples

set.seed(8)
hh <- sample(1:400, 300, TRUE, prob = rgamma(400, 0.5))
day <- sort(sample(1:365, 300, TRUE))
rptvic(hh, t = day, pop = 1000, brk = c(0, 7, 30, 90, 365))
#> rptvic: 300 incidents, 155 victims, 145 repeats (48.3%)
#>  k victims incidents     expected
#>  0     845         0 7.408182e+02
#>  1      77        77 2.222455e+02
#>  2      42        84 3.333682e+01
#>  3      19        57 3.333682e+00
#>  4       8        32 2.500261e-01
#>  5       6        30 1.500157e-02
#>  6       1         6 7.500784e-04
#>  7       2        14 3.214622e-05
#>  lo  hi  n      share        cum
#>   0   7  9 0.06206897 0.06206897
#>   7  30 26 0.17931034 0.24137931
#>  30  90 58 0.40000000 0.64137931
#>  90 365 52 0.35862069 1.00000000
